proposedDescription: Cheeseweed mallow gets its name from its round, segmented fruits, which look like tiny wheels of cheese. This annual herb grows in gardens, cultivated ground and other disturbed places, with rounded, shallowly lobed leaves and small pale flowers tucked beside the leaf stalks. Its deep taproot becomes woody as the plant matures. Seeds have tough coats and can remain in the soil, so removing young plants before they fruit is much easier than tackling an established patch.
identification: Rounded scalloped leaves; tiny white to pale mauve flowers; wrinkled, wheel-shaped fruits distinguish it from common mallow.
actions: Pull or hoe seedlings while small, removing the taproot before seeds develop. Mowing alone often leaves live buds.
researchNotes: Two independent accounts were directly read. Regional impacts are kept within the source geography; action guidance is precautionary where no species-specific control method is cited.

proposedDescription: Cherokee rose is a vigorous scrambling shrub whose long, hooked canes climb through nearby vegetation. Large white flowers with golden centers stand out against glossy leaves, usually divided into three leaflets; bristly orange-red hips follow. Despite its common name, the plant is native to parts of Asia and was brought to North America during colonial times. It can spread aggressively in the southeastern United States, where a locally native climbing plant is often a better garden choice.
identification: Glossy three-part leaves, hooked prickles, large single white flowers and bristly hips.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves around the canes. Avoid new planting in regions where it spreads aggressively.
researchNotes: Two independent accounts were directly read. Regional impacts are kept within the source geography; action guidance is precautionary where no species-specific control method is cited.

proposedDescription: Cherry bark tortrix is a small, intricately patterned moth whose caterpillars live beneath tree bark. Cherries, plums, apples and other members of the rose family can serve as hosts. Eggs are laid on bark, often near wounds, and the larvae tunnel below the surface, causing cracking and sometimes conspicuous gum. The insect is established in parts of the Pacific Northwest. An adult moth may be easy to overlook; damaged bark near the base of a tree can be the first useful clue.
identification: Brownish forewings patterned with orange and metallic markings; pale larvae beneath loose or cracked bark.
actions: Photograph the trunk damage and contact an extension diagnostician. Avoid moving infested nursery trees or bark to new sites.

proposedDescription: Cherry laurel is a dense evergreen shrub or small tree with broad, glossy leaves and upright clusters of fragrant white flowers. Its dark fruits attract birds, which carry the seeds beyond planted hedges. In the Puget Sound region, escaped plants can thrive in forest shade and crowd native shrubs and tree seedlings. Branches touching the ground can also take root. Cutting a large plant once seldom finishes the job, because both roots and cut stems can produce new growth.
identification: Thick evergreen leaves with glands underneath near the midrib; upright white flower clusters and purple-black fruits.
actions: Dig small plants when soil is moist and watch for seedlings. Plan follow-up for cut stumps; keep foliage and fruit away from people or animals that might eat them.

proposedDescription: Cherry plum is a small deciduous tree that flowers early, often as its first leaves unfold. The species has green leaves and white blossoms, although familiar garden cultivars may have deep purple foliage and pink flowers. Small, smooth-skinned plums range from yellow to red and attract birds. Native to southeastern Europe and parts of Asia, it has escaped cultivation in several regions, including parts of the United States and southeastern Australia. A purple leaf alone identifies neither the species nor its local ecological impact.
identification: Finely toothed oval leaves, five-petaled spring flowers and small rounded plums; leaf color varies by cultivar.
actions: Photograph flowers, leaves and fruit together for identification. Check nearby uncultivated ground for volunteer seedlings before allowing a planting to spread.

proposedDescription: Chestnut blight is caused by a fungus that grows in the bark of chestnut trees. Infection can expand around a branch or trunk, interrupting its supply of water and nutrients and leaving wilted brown leaves above the damaged area. Sunken or cracked cankers may carry tiny orange fruiting bodies. The disease transformed eastern North American forests by devastating American chestnut. It also affects European sweet chestnut; ongoing breeding work seeks useful resistance, but an apparently healthy tree is not proof of lasting protection.
identification: Chestnut bark cankers, orange fungal structures, persistent wilted leaves above damage and new shoots below it; laboratory diagnosis separates look-alike diseases.
actions: Ask an extension or tree-health service to assess suspected cankers. Do not move suspect chestnut bark, wood or nursery plants.
researchNotes: Two independent accounts were directly read. Regional impacts are kept within the source geography; action guidance is precautionary where no species-specific control method is cited.

proposedDescription: Chestnut brown rot can hide inside a nut that looks ordinary from the outside. This fungus damages chestnut kernels, which may become brown, chalky or sponge-like, reducing the quality of the harvest. It can also live in apparently healthy flowers and shoots, and has been associated with twig cankers. Research in Portugal confirmed that isolates caused disease in several sweet-chestnut varieties. Because other fungi produce similar symptoms, a cut nut or bark lesion is a starting point for diagnosis rather than a reliable identification on its own.
identification: Brown or pale chalky decay inside chestnut kernels; shoot cankers may occur, but testing is needed to identify the fungus.
actions: Set aside representative affected nuts and ask a plant diagnostic laboratory for sampling instructions before moving nursery or grafting material.
researchNotes: EPPO now treats this as Sirococcus smithogilvyi (moved in 2026); catalog ID retained. Historical UK pest status is not treated as current. Two independent accounts read; no unsupported home treatment offered.

proposedDescription: Chicory brings clear blue flowers to many roadsides and old fields, opening its flower heads along stiff, branching stems. Young plants begin as a rosette of leaves that can resemble a dandelion, above a substantial taproot with milky sap. This Eurasian plant has a long history of cultivation for leaves and roots, and is now naturalized widely in North America. Wild chicory favors disturbed ground and usually does not move far into undisturbed habitats. Its flowers often close around midday.
identification: Blue, strap-flowered heads along wiry stems; dandelion-like basal leaves and smaller leaves clasping the upper stems.
actions: Confirm the plant before removing garden volunteers. Where unwanted, prevent seed production and remove the root rather than only clipping the flower stalk.

proposedDescription: Chickenspike is an annual wetland herb with soft, upright stems and narrow flower spikes that rise above its leaves. The tiny white flowers are packed closely together, followed by small capsules containing numerous seeds. It grows in shallow water, ditches and flooded ground, and is familiar as a rice-field weed. Its native range spans tropical Africa, Asia and northern Australia. The fleshy lower stem and dense, tapering flower spike are useful clues when examining a plant at the water's edge.

actions: Photograph the whole plant and flower spike without carrying wet soil or seed-bearing material between fields.

proposedDescription: Chickpea milkvetch, also called cicer milkvetch, is a long-lived perennial legume grown for forage and soil stabilization. Its leafy stems carry many paired leaflets and clusters of pale yellow to white pea flowers. The inflated pods darken as they mature, and loose seeds may rattle inside. Native to Europe and the Caucasus region, it spreads through underground shoots as well as seed. Its agricultural usefulness is well documented; its presence in this catalog should not be read as proof that it is invasive everywhere.

actions: Confirm identification before treating a forage stand. Monitor the edges of plantings for seedling or underground-shoot spread.

proposedDescription: Chilean evening primrose opens yellow flowers that take on orange or reddish tones as they age. It begins with a rosette of narrow leaves, then sends up a leafy flowering stem from a stout taproot. actions: If an unwanted garden escape is confirmed, remove it before capsules mature and keep seed-bearing waste contained.

proposedDescription: Chilean gunnera makes a striking clump of enormous, rough-edged leaves on stout, prickly stalks. Despite the nickname giant rhubarb, it is not culinary rhubarb. Its leaves die back seasonally, leaving large buds on thick rhizomes ready for new growth. In invaded areas of Ireland it forms dense colonies in wet ground, along waterways and on coastal sites, shading smaller plants. Other large gunneras, including garden hybrids, can look similar, so the familiar umbrella-shaped leaf is only the beginning of an identification.

proposedDescription: Chilean jessamine is a woody shrub with narrow, glossy leaves and clusters of slender yellow-green flowers. proposedDescription: The Chilean recluse is a brown spider native to South America that has also been introduced elsewhere. It favors sheltered spaces, and established populations outside its native range are sometimes confined to buildings. Its body and legs may be yellowish, reddish brown or darker, with a violin-like marking that can be less obvious than that of the familiar brown recluse. proposedDescription: Chinese banyan can begin life perched on another tree, then develop into a broad evergreen with hanging aerial roots. Some of those roots reach the ground and become pillar-like supports. Its smooth gray bark, leathery leaves and small rounded figs are familiar features of warm-climate plantings. The species is also widely grown as a houseplant and bonsai. proposedDescription: Chinese fir is an evergreen conifer with a tall, tapering crown and spreading branches whose tips often droop. proposedDescription: Chinaberry is a deciduous tree with a spreading crown, finely divided leaves and fragrant lilac-colored flowers. proposedDescription: Chinese firethorn is a spiny shrub grown for its clusters of white flowers and bright red fruits. proposedDescription: Chinese lovegrass is a small tuft-forming grass whose open seed heads carry flattened clusters of tiny flowers. These spikelets can turn purplish red as they mature, giving the airy heads a subtle wash of color. Its stems may rise from a leaning base, and plants grow as annuals or short-lived perennials. Native across tropical and subtropical Asia into parts of Queensland, it occurs in grasslands and along roadsides. Similar lovegrasses are difficult to separate, so close views of mature spikelets are more useful than a distant photograph.
identification: Open branched seed heads and flattened, many-flowered spikelets that may mature purplish red. A grass specialist should compare the spikelets and leaf joints.

proposedDescription: Chinese mitten crab is named for the dense bristles that cover its claws like fuzzy gloves. Rounded whorls, freshwater habitats, grazing and live birth

proposedDescription: Chinese raspwort is a small perennial of wet tropical regions, native from southern China through parts of Southeast Asia and the Pacific to Australia. It is easy to overlook beside larger wetland plants. The New South Wales form has rough, four-ribbed stems, narrow toothed leaves and tiny flowers followed by ribbed fruits. Its Australian subspecies is treated separately in this collection, so a close look at the fruit matters when putting a precise name to a plant.
identification: In the NSW account, plants have four-ribbed stems, opposite lower leaves and tiny eight-ribbed fruits. Subspecies determination requires mature fruit.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, stem, leaves and mature fruits. Ask a herbarium to check the subspecies before recommending removal.
researchNotes: NSW morphology refers to subsp. verrucosus, the only NSW subspecies. Broad distribution follows Kew; introduced status is not itself evidence of ecological harm.

claims: Accepted perennial; native southern China to Caroline Islands and Australia; two subspecies
Regional morphology and wet coastal habitat; NSW plants are subsp. verrucosus

proposedDescription: This Australian subspecies of Chinese raspwort is a slender perennial of damp, open ground. Its small toothed leaves sit mostly in opposite pairs on rough, four-ribbed stems, and the flowers are tiny enough to need a close look. The rounded fruits carry eight ribs, small bumps and short curved hairs, useful details for a careful identification. Native to eastern Australia, it has also been introduced to California and Hawaii; that history alone does not establish how it affects a particular wetland.
identification: Plants about 20-45 cm tall; narrow toothed leaves and tiny ribbed, bumpy fruits with short curved hairs.
actions: Record mature fruit details and habitat without disturbing the wetland. Confirm local status and identity before control.
researchNotes: ID retains the supplied ssp spelling. Accepted botanical rank is subsp. verrucosus. No species-wide invasion impact or control efficacy was established.

claims: Habit, leaves, ribbed hairy fruits and wet open habitat
Accepted subspecies, eastern Australian origin and introductions to California and Hawaii

proposedDescription: Chinese rose beetles often reveal themselves through the lace-like holes they leave between leaf veins. Adults emerge after dusk to feed on many kinds of plants, including garden ornamentals and crops. They are small brown scarabs covered with pale hairs, while their whitish grubs develop underground. The beetle is usually called Adoretus sinicus in modern identification guides. Because a close relative looks almost identical, feeding damage and a photograph can suggest an identification but may not settle it.
identification: Brown oval scarab about 10-12 mm long with pale hairs and three outer teeth on the front tibia; expert examination separates A. compressus.
actions: Inspect affected plants after dusk, photograph beetles and feeding injury, and seek local identification before treatment.
researchNotes: Lepadoretus sinicus is explicitly listed as a synonym of Adoretus sinicus by Bigger. Soil larvae are not assigned unsupported root damage.

claims: Adult morphology, dusk feeding, broad host range and externally similar A. compressus
Night feeding and characteristic holes between veins
Page 82 explicitly links Lepadoretus sinicus to Adoretus sinicus

proposedDescription: Chinese silvergrass forms tall, arching clumps topped by airy flower plumes. Familiar from ornamental plantings, this Asian perennial can send windborne seeds beyond the garden and establish along roadsides and other disturbed ground. Older clumps develop a substantial underground mass that makes removal difficult. Cultivars differ in size, leaf pattern and fertility, so a garden label is worth keeping, but it does not replace checking for seedlings nearby. In regions where it spreads, a locally appropriate native grass is a better planting choice.
identification: Arching grass clumps, often several feet tall, with feathery flower plumes; leaf stripes and mature size vary among cultivars.
actions: Avoid new planting where invasive. Remove escaped seedlings early and obtain local advice for established root masses.
researchNotes: NCSU supports morphology and dispersal; Maryland Extension independently recommends avoiding invasive ornamental grasses. No universal fertility claim is made for cultivars.

claims: Asian clumping perennial, wind-dispersed seeds, rhizome mass and variable cultivars
Miscanthus sinensis identified among invasive ornamental grasses to avoid

proposedDescription: Chinese tallow is often noticed for its autumn color and clusters of white seeds that resemble popcorn. The deciduous tree has broadly rounded leaves drawn out into slender tips and produces yellow flower spikes in spring. Brought from Asia as an ornamental and potential crop, it now invades wetlands, prairies and forests in the southeastern United States. Birds and water carry its seeds, while cut trees can sprout again. Removing seedlings early and planning follow-up for larger trees helps prevent a return.
identification: Alternate simple leaves with rounded bases and long tips; milky sap; three-part capsules opening to white seeds.
actions: Pull small seedlings before seed production. Use qualified help for mature trees and plan for stump sprouts and later seedlings.
researchNotes: Regional invasion and management are supported by UF/IFAS and the USDA synthesis. Historical distribution lists are not presented as current county evidence.

claims: Leaf and seed identification, bird/water dispersal, seedling removal and stump resprouting
Asian origin and invasion of southeastern wetlands, prairies and forests

proposedDescription: Chinese violet is a creeping perennial with opposite leaves, trumpet-shaped flowers and seed capsules that spring open when ripe. Garden forms can spread quickly in warm climates. The name covers more than one subspecies: the small white flowers with purple markings belong to subsp. micrantha, a serious smothering weed in parts of Australia, while other forms have larger, differently colored flowers. Stems can root where they touch moist soil, making dumped cuttings an effective way to start a new patch.
identification: Opposite egg-shaped leaves and trumpet flowers. Small white flowers with two purple blotches suggest subsp. micrantha; confirm with fruit and flower details.
actions: Keep cut stems out of garden dumping areas and waterways. Where removal is appropriate, collect roots and stem fragments and check for regrowth.
researchNotes: NSW impact and rooting guidance specifically concern subsp. micrantha. NParks species-level horticultural account supplies the broader flower, leaf and capsule context.

claims: Creeping perennial, opposite leaves, trumpet flowers and explosively opening capsules
Subspecies distinctions, smothering impacts, rooting stem fragments and removal guidance

proposedDescription: Chinese wisteria's fragrant spring flower clusters can be beautiful, but the woody vine grows with enough force to overwhelm trees and shrubs. It climbs by twining and can also spread across the ground, where touching stems take root. The hanging seed pods are velvety, unlike those of native American wisteria. Escaped vines can shade woodland plants and tighten around their supports. Successful removal usually takes follow-up because cutting an established vine commonly produces fresh shoots.
identification: Woody counterclockwise-twining vine; spring blue-violet flower clusters and velvety pods. Native American wisteria has smooth pods and generally blooms later.
actions: Avoid planting near natural areas. Cut accessible stems carefully and arrange repeated follow-up; obtain local guidance for established infestations.
researchNotes: NCSU and Maryland Extension directly support biology and impacts. Cutting is not described as a one-time cure, and no pesticide recipe is supplied.

claims: Chinese origin, woody twining habit, fragrant spring flowers and velvety fruit
Rooting stems, woodland suppression, native comparison and resprouting after cutting

proposedDescription: Dioscorea oppositifolia is a tuber-forming climbing yam native to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar. Its name has often been applied incorrectly to Chinese yam in North American writing. That distinction matters: descriptions of the invasive Chinese yam cannot simply be transferred to this species. This record needs its scientific name and intended common name reconciled before a reliable field guide or removal recommendation can be attached to it.
identification: The supplied scientific name and Chinese yam label do not reliably identify the same taxon; do not diagnose it from Chinese yam field marks.
actions: Have the original taxon record checked before applying Chinese yam control advice or changing a species identification.
researchNotes: Research gap: Kew accepts D. oppositifolia for an Indian-subcontinent/Myanmar species; USDA explicitly flags its misapplication to Chinese yam. Preserve ID pending editorial taxonomy decision.

claims: Accepted climbing tuberous species native Indian subcontinent to Myanmar
D. oppositifolia has been consistently misapplied to North American Chinese yam

proposedDescription: Chinese yellowcress is a small annual mustard native to eastern Asia. Its lower leaves are divided into lobes, while the smaller leaves higher on the stem clasp it at their bases. Small flowers give way to short, slender cylindrical seed pods. A close look is worthwhile because several yellowcresses share this modest appearance, and leaf shape changes as the plant grows. Photographs showing both the low leaves and mature pods are much more useful than a single flower portrait.
identification: Hairless herb with lobed lower leaves, clasping upper leaves and cylindrical pods about 6-8 mm long in the Shanghai flora.
actions: Document basal leaves and mature fruit for expert identification. Check regional status before deciding whether removal is warranted.
researchNotes: Kew supports native range and annual habit; Shanghai botanical-garden flora supplies morphology. No unsupported North American impact or control claim is included.

claims: Accepted annual native Vietnam to Russian Far East and temperate East Asia
Lobed basal leaves, clasping stem leaves, hairless habit and cylindrical fruit

proposedDescription: Chir pine is a tall Himalayan pine with notably long needles carried in bundles of three. Its elongated, egg-shaped woody cones are another useful feature, especially when compared with the shorter cones of some familiar landscape pines. Native from Pakistan through the Himalaya and northern India, it has long been valued as a source of resin. A planted tree is not by itself evidence of an invasion; seedlings growing beyond cultivation deserve a separate, locally informed assessment.
identification: Long needles in bundles of three, non-resinous winter buds and elongated ovoid cones; compare cones and needle bundles with other pines.
actions: Record cones, needle bundles and any independently growing seedlings. Consult regional forestry guidance before removing or planting trees.
researchNotes: Botanical sources establish identity and native range, not broad invasive impact. Nursery and spontaneous occurrences must remain distinct.

claims: Long needles in threes, large elongated cones, tall habit and resin use
Accepted tree native Pakistan to Himalaya and northwestern India

proposedDescription: The chocolate moth, also called the cacao or tobacco moth, is a small moth associated with stored goods. Its larvae feed in products such as cocoa, tobacco, cereals and dried foods, so an indoor sighting is a reason to inspect supplies rather than assume the moth came from the garden. Adults have a wingspan of roughly 15-20 millimeters and resemble several related warehouse moths. Warm storage conditions allow populations to develop more quickly, and a precise identification may require an expert.
identification: Small pale warehouse moth, roughly 15-20 mm wingspan; similar Ephestia species can require examination of genitalia.
actions: Inspect stored products and keep suspect stock separate while identification and appropriate storage-pest management are arranged.
researchNotes: INRAE and UKMoths independently describe the stored-product association. No unsupported worldwide phenology or insecticide guidance is inferred.

claims: Larval damage to tobacco and dried products; faster multiplication in warmth
Wingspan, warehouse association and resemblance to E. parasitella

proposedDescription: Chocolate vine has five smooth leaflets arranged like the fingers of a hand and small, dark, fragrant flowers in spring. This woody climber comes from eastern Asia and can grow rapidly over shrubs and other vegetation. Its unusual purple fruits may split open to reveal pale pulp and dark seeds, which birds can carry elsewhere. In mild climates it keeps much of its foliage through winter. Once established, repeated pruning may not be enough to contain it, making early attention to escapes worthwhile.
identification: Palmately arranged groups of five leaflets; twining woody stems, reddish-purple spring flowers and elongated purple fruits.
actions: Avoid new planting where invasive. Check nearby vegetation for escaped stems and seedlings and seek a removal plan for established vines.
researchNotes: NCSU detailed account is independently supported by Maryland Extension's invasive-vine planting advice. Fruit production is not assumed for every garden specimen.

claims: Five leaflets, fragrant flowers, fruit, rapid growth and bird-dispersed seeds
Chocolate vine is included among invasive vines to avoid planting

proposedDescription: Chocolateweed is a small upright herb or subshrub with toothed leaves and tight clusters of little flowers. Despite its common name, the flowers may be white, pink or purple, with regional variation described in botanical floras. Rounded, hairy capsules follow the blooms. The plant occurs widely across warm parts of the Old World and Australia, including damp or seasonally wet places. Its name should not be taken as proof that every population is unwanted: it is native in parts of its range.
identification: Toothed oval to narrow leaves, clustered small flowers and rounded hairy capsules; flower color varies among regional accounts.
actions: Photograph leaves, flower clusters and fruit. Confirm local native status and land-management needs before removing a population.
researchNotes: Kew's African floras and Western Australian Herbarium provide independently authored morphology. Color variation is retained instead of forcing agreement; no invasion severity is assumed.

proposedDescription: Christmas candlestick stands out for the rounded clusters of orange flowers spaced along its upright stems. Also called lion's tail, it has opposite toothed leaves and can grow taller than a person in warm conditions. Botanical accounts place its native range in Africa and the Indian subcontinent. Introduced populations can form large colonies; a Queensland management account describes displacement of native vegetation along riverbanks and floodplains. Seeds can travel in water or muddy equipment, so keeping them on site matters during removal.
identification: Tall herb with opposite toothed leaves and globular clusters of orange, hairy flowers surrounded by pointed floral structures.
actions: Where control is needed, remove young plants before seed production and clean soil from equipment. Revisit the patch for seedlings.
researchNotes: Native range follows current Kew rather than older Australian claims of American origin. Townsville 2004-2008 plan supports morphology, spread and regional impact only, not current law or distribution.

proposedDescription: Christmas grass is a tufted tropical grass whose seed heads reward a closer look. Small groups of spikelets sit within papery bracts, and each fertile unit carries a conspicuous bent, twisted bristle. Most leaves arise near the base of the plant. Native across parts of tropical Asia to northern Australia, it belongs to the same genus as other grasses that can look similar from a distance. Mature flowering material is therefore much more useful for identification than a photograph of the leaves alone.
identification: Tufted grass with mostly basal leaves; enclosed spikelet clusters and long, bent, twisted awns, often 5-9 cm long.
actions: Photograph mature seed heads and the whole clump. Seek a grass specialist's confirmation before control or moving seed-bearing material.
researchNotes: Kew WCVP supports native range; AusGrass supplies morphology. GrassBase and AusGrass share descriptive conventions, so the duplicated morphology is not treated as independent corroboration. No invasion-impact claim is made.

claims: Tufted habit, basal leaves, enclosed spikelet clusters and long twisted awns
Native range from Sri Lanka to northern Australia and wet tropical occurrence

proposedDescription: Chrysanthemum aphids gather around tender shoots, buds and leaf undersides, where they feed on plant sap. The small adults are dark reddish brown to nearly black; younger aphids are often dull brick red. Colonies can build quickly because females give birth to live young, and infested plants can carry them between greenhouses. Feeding may distort or stunt growth, while sticky honeydew supports black sooty mold. Regularly checking new shoots and incoming plants helps catch a colony before it becomes dense.
identification: Dark aphids with short black cornicles; wingless adults about 1.5 mm, nymphs brick red; colonies concentrate on chrysanthemum growth.
actions: Inspect chrysanthemums weekly and separate incoming plants for inspection. Remove heavily infested plants and seek crop-specific advice while conserving natural enemies.
researchNotes: Minnesota PDF reproduces NC State AG-136 and is credited to that source group, not counted as a separate Minnesota study. Kansas State 2026 is independent.

sources.title: NC State AG-136 via University of Minnesota

claims: Dark adults, rapid live reproduction, honeydew, stunting, plant transport and weekly scouting

evidence.independentSourceGroup: NC State AG-136 via University of Minnesota
claims: Adult/nymph identification, terminal feeding, distortion and greenhouse life cycle

proposedDescription: Cigarette beetles are tiny, rounded, reddish-brown insects that can turn up in far more than tobacco. Their larvae feed in dried products, including spices, grains, pet food and other stored plant material. The adult's head is tucked beneath its thorax, giving it a hooded appearance from above. Fine details help separate it from the similar drugstore beetle: cigarette beetles have saw-toothed antennae and lack rows of pits on their wing covers. Finding the infested material is more useful than treating a wandering adult.
identification: About 3 mm long, rounded and reddish brown; serrated antennae and smooth-looking wing covers distinguish it from drugstore beetle.
actions: Inspect dry goods and stored plant material, isolate suspect packages and ask an Extension or pest professional to identify the source.
researchNotes: Purdue's 3 mm value is used; its inconsistent inch conversion is omitted. INRAE independently supports stored-product biology. Professional fumigation is not presented as a home action.

claims: Adult identification, drugstore-beetle distinction and broad dried-product hosts
Reddish adults and larval tunneling in stored tobacco and other dry materials

proposedDescription: True cinnamon is the Sri Lankan tree whose bark supplies the familiar spice. Fresh leaves often emerge red before turning glossy green, and several strong veins run from near the leaf base toward the tip. Small pale flowers are followed by dark, fleshy, single-seeded fruits. In tropical gardens the tree can become a substantial evergreen. Because other cinnamon relatives share aromatic leaves and bark, a scent alone is a poor identification test; leaf arrangement, veins and fruit provide a better starting point.
identification: Glossy, leathery leaves, reddish new growth and three to five strong basal veins; small pale flowers and dark oval fruits.
actions: Use leaves and fruit for identification rather than tasting bark. Check local guidance before planting and watch for seedlings beyond cultivation.
researchNotes: Kew and NParks support botany and Sri Lankan origin. No health claims or general invasion classification is inferred from spice use.

claims: Red young leaves, opposite leaves with three veins, pale flowers, dark fruit and spice use

proposedDescription: Circular hemlock scale is a tiny armored insect that settles mainly beneath conifer needles. Females sit under rounded, dark brown covers with a raised center; heavy infestations can coat much of a needle. Feeding removes plant fluids and may lead to yellowing and premature needle loss, particularly on hemlocks. Also called shortneedle evergreen scale, it has a mobile crawler stage before the insects settle. Inspecting the lower crown with a hand lens can reveal a problem before thinning foliage becomes obvious.
identification: Female covers circular, dark brown and strongly convex, about 1-1.3 mm wide; usually on needle undersides. Confirm against other armored scales.
actions: Inspect lower needle surfaces with magnification. Have a diagnostic service confirm the scale and time any management to locally observed crawlers.
researchNotes: UMass includes original diagnostic confirmation and management synthesis; ScaleNet contributes Marlatt's morphology and host catalogue. Connecticut timing is not generalized nationally.

claims: Needle position, yellowing/drop, crawler biology and monitoring lower crowns
Circular convex dark female cover and conifer host records
